name: Chlorophyll internal deodorant
lead: Chlorophyll internal deodorant refers to the oral use of chlorophyll or its water-soluble semi-synthetic derivatives, chlorophyllins, to reduce body, breath or waste odour. People use it so they smell fresher, a part of overall grooming and presentation. Chlorophyllins are salts made from chlorophyll, and the main food-additive forms are sodium chlorophyllins, listed as E140(ii) and E141(ii) [1].

Oral preparations have been marketed for odour from incontinence, colostomies and body odour generally [1]. Some people also use chlorophyllin at home for pimples and blackheads, based on its antimicrobial effect [1]. The Wikipedia article on the topic flags the odour claim as lacking medical citation and cites no controlled human trials of body, ostomy or fecal odour [1]. Laboratory and animal research on chlorophyllin has mostly concerned binding of mutagens, such as certain polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, rather than odour [1].

chain: Chlorophyll or chlorophyllin taken by mouth
Less noticeable body or breath odour
angle.text: Users take it hoping to smell cleaner from the inside, an idea promoted since the 1940s and revived as 'chlorophyll water' on social media in the 2020s. It is used alongside, rather than instead of, hygiene products.

paras: In the 1940s the researcher F. Howard Westcott described chlorophyll as an odour blocker. Between about 1950 and 1953 companies added it to toothpaste, sanitary products and soap, mainly in advertising, and brands dropped it quickly afterwards [1]. The Wikipedia article states that the hype was later judged unwarranted and that the underlying research may have been a hoax [1].
In the 2020s social media influencers revived it as 'chlorophyll water'; Wikipedia describes the medical claims made for it as unsubstantiated [1].

In laboratory settings chlorophyllin binds to some environmental mutagens. Studies, largely in cells and animals, report protective effects against food-additive-induced genotoxicity and mitochondrial dysfunction, and it has been reported to modulate certain cytokines [1]. These findings do not address odour.
Body-odour guidance lists chlorophyllin ointments, sprays and supplements among agents that have been used, alongside antiperspirants, deodorants and antibacterial soaps [2].
No studies found. The Wikipedia entry cites no controlled human trials of chlorophyllin for body, ostomy or fecal odour; related research is in vitro or animal work on other effects [1].

timeline.event: F. Howard Westcott's research describes chlorophyll as an odour blocker.[1]
Chlorophyll used in toothpaste, sanitary towels and soap marketing.[1]
Revived on social media as 'chlorophyll water'.[1]

card.summary: Oral chlorophyll or chlorophyllin pitched as an internal deodorant; the cited human evidence for body odor is essentially absent.
card.note: No controlled human trials for body odor found in cited sources.

quick.overview:
Chlorophyll and chlorophyllin are green plant-pigment products sold as oral 'internal deodorants' for body, breath and waste odor. The idea dates to the 1940s and returned via social media in the 2020s.

The cited reference material lists no controlled human trials of the odor claim.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say it neutralizes odor-causing compounds from within. Laboratory research has shown chlorophyllin binding some mutagens, but this has not been shown to apply to body odor.
quick.risks: The cited sources contain no safety discussion. It is sold as a supplement and used as a food colorant (E140/E141).
